implementation_notes: Ruby provides the completion half (Thread#join, #value) and a useful wake-up primitive (Thread::Queue#close makes a blocked deq return nil once the queue is drained), but the stop request itself is hand-written, so the classic structure survives: an idempotent flag or a closed queue is phase 1, the worker's own ensure block does the cleanup, and join is phase 2 - the docs are explicit that threads not joined are killed when the main program exits. The tempting shortcuts are the reason this is manual: Thread#kill and Thread#raise are asynchronous interrupts that can land anywhere, including inside rescue/ensure while resources are half-released, which is why the docs provide Thread.handle_interrupt to guard deallocation; they are forced-stop mechanisms, not a clean second phase.
code_sketch:
jobs = Thread::Queue.new
worker = Thread.new do
  begin
    while (job = jobs.deq)               # nil once closed and drained
      handle(job)
    end
  ensure
    flush_and_release                     # phase 2 cleanup, all exit paths
  end
end

jobs.close                                # phase 1: stop after the buffer drains
worker.join                               # phase 2: cleanup finished
pitfalls: Thread#kill and Thread#raise may be delivered inside rescue/ensure while resources are half-released (the docs' Thread.handle_interrupt example exists exactly to defend against this), so they must not be the normal shutdown path.
Any thread not joined is killed when the main program exits, mid-cleanup: join the workers before leaving the process, including in scripts and Rake tasks.
A worker blocked on a Queue pop or sleep only sees the request when the blocking call returns; close the queue (or use a timeout/non-blocking deq) as the wake-up instead of relying on the flag alone.
Queue#close is one-way and permanent: a closed queue cannot be reopened, so restarts need a fresh queue rather than a reset.
